extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mathematics/geometry (including historians of mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and classification of proportion and proportionality in classical geometry: definitions, types (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic), continuous vs discrete proportions, commensurability/incommensurability, and applications to measurement and the arts. The text develops definitions, examples, and methods for determining and comparing proportions (following Euclidean tradition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proportion / proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion (la proportione, la proportionalita) is the relation between quantities — one quantity to another — expressing comparative magnitude; it can be presented in numbers, measures, or magnitudes and is the foundational relation used to compare lines, areas, volumes, numbers, times, places, weights, and powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that proportion is found not only among numbers and measures but among many kinds of quantities (lines, surfaces, bodies, times, places, weights, powers). It distinguishes ways to express and reason about proportion (e.g., using Euclidean propositions) and notes that knowing proportions is necessary for many practical arts and sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of proportion: arithmetic, geometric, harmonic
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions are classified into arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic (aritmetica, geometrica, harmonica). Arithmetic proportion commonly concerns numbers and their differences; geometric proportion concerns magnitudes and ratio relations (often continuous); harmonic proportion concerns relations relevant to sound/music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes when each type arises: arithmetic in discrete numbers and numerical operations, geometric in magnitudes and continuous ratios (lines, areas), and harmonic particularly in musical contexts (tones/notes). It also indicates subdivisions (e.g., harmonic has arithmetical and geometrical subcases) and that one should identify which type applies when comparing quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous vs discrete (continua e discreta) proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous proportion arises among continuous magnitudes (lines, surfaces, bodies, times) and often involves sequences or interpolations across multiple terms; a discrete proportion pertains to discrete numbers or units where comparisons are via whole-number ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous proportions may require at least three or four terms (interpolations) and can be infinite in progression; discrete (arithmetical) proportions use distinct integer relationships. The text explains when to treat a proportion as continuous versus discrete and how this affects methods of comparison and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurable vs incommensurable quantities (misurabili vs incommeasurabili)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commensurable quantities are those sharing a common measure so a definite common unit can measure them exactly; incommensurable quantities lack a common measure (e.g., diameter and side of a square), so no finite common measure exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and Euclidean references are given (diameter vs side of a square). The text distinguishes measures that admit a common unit (commensurable) from those that do not (incommensurable) and explains consequences for forming definite numerical ratios or denominating a proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and inequality of proportions (equalitas / inequalitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional relations may be equal or unequal; equality of proportion occurs when the comparative relation of terms is the same, while inequality can be expressed as greater/less (with further distinctions like greater inequality and lesser inequality, depending on which term is referred to which).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise gives number examples illustrating equal proportion (e.g., 4:4) and different forms of inequality (examples using sequences like 2:1, 1:8, etc.), and discusses how to compare magnitudes or numbers by referring larger to smaller and vice versa (father to son, lord to servant) producing different named forms of inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean / mediate proportion and related subtypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and roles of mediate (mean) and immediate proportions: mediate proportion refers to terms between extremes; other named forms (e.g., double/doppia, duplicate/duplicata) describe specific proportional relationships such as those between diameters and squares or between sides and their squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text ties these definitions to Euclidean propositions (e.g., proposition about the diameter and side of a square; duplicate proportion where one term is double another in the square). It shows how such named proportions arise in geometric contexts and how they are used to determine relations among magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for determining/proving proportions (use of common measure, multiplication, interpolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions can be established or found by use of a common measure, by multiplying/dividing terms appropriately, or by interpolation between terms in a sequence; merchants and craftsmen use proportional calculations to determine prices, sizes, or otherwise scale quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical procedures are discussed: finding the unknown number by setting a proper proportion (multiplying/dividing terms), using the rule of three/multiplicative methods, or applying common measures to check commensurability. Examples include merchants finding prices and artisans scaling materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of proportion to the arts and crafts (architecture, painting, tailoring, woodwork)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper proportion is required in applied arts: architecture (harmonious temple proportions), painting (proportionate depiction of human figures and parts), tailoring (cutting cloth proportional to length/width), and mechanical crafts (machines, naval parts) — in each case proportions must be 'debet' (proper) to the function and appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text elaborates many concrete examples: architecture following Vitruvius (temples, fronts), painting where parts of a figure must be placed with due proportion, clothing where length/width of cloth must be proportionate to the designed garment, and tools/machinery sized with proper proportion for effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of proportional relations by roles of terms (extremes and means; reference directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportion is expressed between extremes and means; the way one term is referred to another (e.g., larger to smaller, nearer to nearer) matters and changes the named relation. The same four terms can produce different named proportions depending on which are taken as extremes and which as means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes the importance of which terms are compared (extreme vs mean), and that referring different terms (e.g., father to son vs son to father) yields different proportional relations and names. It gives examples and recommends careful attention to the order and reference when defining a proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Euclidean propositions and classical terminology for proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional reasoning is grounded in Euclid's definitions and propositions: many statements refer to Euclid's propositions (definitions of proportion, measurability, and relations between lines and their squares), and the text adopts Euclidean vocabulary and logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly cites Euclid (e.g., proposition numbers) as justification/examples (diameter and square, duplicate proportion), and instructs the reader to use those classical results when reasoning about proportions, commensurability, and types of proportional relations.
